title: Takeaway and restaurant grease traps overfill between pump-outs, and water companies prosecute under s111 for the sewer blockages
problem: A takeaway's grease trap fills with fat, oil and grease (FOG) weeks before the contractor's next scheduled pump-out. Fat bypasses into the public sewer, blocks it and floods the street or a watercourse. Water companies now prosecute under s111 Water Industry Act: Severn Trent and Thames Water cases came to ~£5.5k–£13k in fines and costs, one of them after a trap had already been fitted. On top come blockage-clearance recharges and re-inspections, and the owner can't show the trap was being maintained.
who_suffers: Food-outlet owners and managers; water-company sewer network teams; residents whose streets flood
buyer: Operations director of a grease-management or drainage service company that bills per pump-out, or ops director of a multi-site takeaway or restaurant franchise
industry: FOG management for food outlets discharging to public sewers
current_workaround: Fixed-interval pump-outs (4–12 weekly) regardless of how full the trap is, paper service dockets, and water-company FOG inspectors lifting covers after a blockage
sensor_concept: Time-of-flight or ultrasonic distance sensor in the trap lid reads the standing liquid level (a rising level means the outlet is choking with fat). A lid reed switch logs each service and a temperature probe catches hot-fat dumps. LTE-M, battery. The contractor is alerted to book an early pump-out, and every service is auto-logged as evidence for FOG inspectors.
notes: c1/c4/c10 strong: named s111 prosecutions with £ figures and water-company FOG campaigns. c6 strong: pump-out contractors already visit and bill per visit. c7 risk: GreaseBoss sells trap sensors mainly in Australia, so the UK gap needs verifying.

title: Holiday parks and rural venues on private boreholes: the UV steriliser lamp fails silently and E. coli turns up in the council's sample
problem: Commercial private water supplies (holiday parks, campsites, wedding venues, farm shops) depend on a UV unit. Lamps lose output after ~9,000 hours or stay off after a power cut, and only a small local LED shows it. Council sampling under the Private Water Supplies Regulations 2016 then finds E. coli. A Regulation 18 notice can restrict use, guests get boil-water notices or bottled water, and illness complaints and refunds follow. Council sampling and re-sampling fees run to ~£ hundreds per visit.
who_suffers: Guests and staff drinking the water; the business owner facing notices and refunds
buyer: Owner or operations manager of a holiday park, campsite or rural venue group on a private supply
industry: Commercial private water supplies regulated under the Private Water Supplies Regulations 2016 (Regulation 9 supplies)
current_workaround: Annual lamp change by a water-treatment engineer, a glance at the UV unit's LED when someone remembers, and council sampling once or more a year
sensor_concept: Clip-on current transformer on the UV ballast feed, a low-cost UV-C photodiode at the sleeve viewport, and a pulse or flow switch on the outlet. The unit alarms if water flows while the lamp is off or its output is low. LTE-M. Produces a monthly log for the council risk assessment.
notes: c4 strong: PWS Regs 2016, DWI annual reports on failures, local-authority notices. c6 via water-treatment service firms that change lamps every year. c8 simple (CT plus photodiode). c1 is weaker unless outbreak or claim figures are found.

title: Bowsers for alternative water supply run dry, get tipped over or sit unfilled during mains outages, and regulators fine the company for the poor response
problem: When a trunk main bursts, water companies must put out bowsers and bottled-water stations. Nobody can see which bowsers are empty, which were contaminated after vandalism, or which were never refilled, so vulnerable customers go without. In 2026 Ofwat proposed a ~£22m penalty on South East Water, citing shortages of bottled water and tankers in 2020–23 outages. Statutory GSS compensation is also paid per affected household.
who_suffers: Customers without water, especially vulnerable households; incident managers
buyer: Head of alternative water supplies or incident manager at a water company, or ops director of the contracted bowser and tanker provider
industry: Water-company alternative water supply during supply interruptions
current_workaround: Drivers on fixed refill rounds, phone reports from the public, and staff sent out to check each bowser
sensor_concept: Bolt-on ultrasonic level sensor in the bowser lid, GPS, and a tilt or tamper accelerometer (bowser moved, tipped or lid opened). LTE-M/NB-IoT. Gives the incident room a live map, routes refills, and keeps an audit trail for Ofwat and DWI incident reports.
notes: c1/c4/c10 strong: Ofwat enforcement with a £ figure, DWI event reports, press complaints. c2 moderate: several outages a year per company. c8 easy. c5 is the weak point because the buyer is an enterprise utility; the bowser hire contractor may be the better buyer.

title: RPZ backflow valves stick open and dump water through the relief port for months between annual tests
problem: Reduced-pressure-zone (RPZ) valves protect the mains from fluid category 4 risks at car washes, labs, hospitals and chemical-dosing plant, and must be tested at least annually by an accredited tester. When a check valve fouls, the relief port discharges continuously. That can waste ~£ thousands of water a year and flood plant rooms. Some sites bypass a faulty RPZ instead, which is a Water Fittings Regulations offence that water companies inspect for and prosecute.
who_suffers: Site FM teams and owners paying the water bill; the water company protecting the mains
buyer: Owner or ops manager of an accredited backflow-testing or water-hygiene contractor, selling it as a service; or the site's estates manager
industry: Testing and maintenance of backflow prevention devices
current_workaround: Annual RPZ test certificate; nobody looks at the tundish in between
sensor_concept: Two-electrode water-presence sensor or flap-type flow detector in the RPZ tundish or air-gap drain, plus a pipe temperature probe. LoRaWAN or LTE-M. Alerts on sustained discharge, and appends a monthly log to the annual test certificate.
notes: c4 strong: Water Supply (Water Fittings) Regulations 1999 and water-company inspections. c6 strong: accredited testers visit every year and already sell maintenance. c8 trivial sensor. c7 likely unserved. c1 needs sourced figures for water waste and flooding.

title: Cesspools at rural pubs, campsites and wedding venues overflow on busy weekends before the tanker's fixed slot
problem: Off-mains hospitality businesses with sealed cesspools (no outlet) fill them fast during events and peak weekends. Tanker firms empty on a fixed rota at ~£250–£400 a load, so tanks are either emptied half full or overflow. An overflowing cesspool is a pollution offence and a statutory nuisance: EA or council action, clean-up costing ~£ thousands, and toilets closed on the busiest day of the year.
who_suffers: Venue owners; neighbours and watercourses; customers
buyer: Owner or director of a liquid-waste tankering company selling 'empty when needed' contracts, or the venue owner
industry: Cesspool and holding-tank emptying for off-mains commercial premises
current_workaround: Lifting the lid to look, fixed-interval collections, and emergency call-outs at premium rates
sensor_concept: Ultrasonic level sensor through the tank lid, LTE-M. Alerts at 75% and 90% full and forecasts the fill rate so the tanker firm can schedule runs. Every empty is logged to match the waste transfer notes.
notes: c6 strong: tanker firms visit and bill per visit, and route density is their margin. c8 easy. c7 risk from generic tank-level gauges. c1 is moderate unless prosecution figures are found.

title: Illegal water taken from fire hydrants by unlicensed tankers and contractors stirs up sediment and sets off discoloured-water events
problem: Unauthorised hydrant use (tankers, road sweepers, builders without a licensed standpipe) creates pressure transients that mobilise pipe sediment. Whole streets get brown water, which brings DWI event reports, customer compensation and flushing crews, and the water is never billed. Water companies run 'water theft' campaigns and prosecute, but usually only hear about the theft from complaints.
who_suffers: Customers with discoloured water; network operations teams; revenue protection
buyer: Revenue protection or network protection manager at a water company
industry: Water distribution networks: misuse of hydrants and standpipes
current_workaround: Public reports, licensed-standpipe schemes, occasional patrols, and prosecutions after the fact
sensor_concept: Accelerometer and magnetic reed sensor under the hydrant pit cover detect the cover being lifted or the valve spindle turned. A pipe-mounted vibration signature confirms flow. NB-IoT. Sends an alert with location and time so a patrol can attend, and builds an evidence pack for prosecution.
notes: c4/c10: Water Industry Act offences, DWI discolouration events, water-company theft campaigns. c8 simple. Weak on c5 (enterprise utility buyer); worth testing whether a contractor channel exists.

title: Sewer overpumping during pipe repairs relies on paid night-time 'pump watch' staff, and a stalled pump floods homes with sewage
problem: While a sewer is relined or repaired, flows are overpumped round the work with diesel pumps for days or weeks. If a pump stops or runs out of fuel overnight, sewage backs up into gardens and homes. Internal sewer flooding counts against the water company's Ofwat performance commitments, and clean-up and compensation cost ~£ thousands per property, plus EA pollution reports. To prevent this, contractors pay an attendant to sit on site all night.
who_suffers: Residents flooded with sewage; the contractor and the water company client
buyer: Operations manager of a sewer rehabilitation or overpumping contractor
industry: Sewer rehabilitation and temporary overpumping
current_workaround: 24/7 pump-watch attendants, hourly physical checks and fuel top-up rounds
sensor_concept: Clamp-on accelerometer shows the pump running, a float switch in the upstream manhole shows the level rising, and a fuel-tank level sensor tracks fuel. LTE-M, battery. An SMS and call cascade reaches the on-call crew, and an event log goes to the client.
notes: c3 strong: paid attendant labour per night is a quantifiable workaround. c6 good via overpumping hire firms. c7 risk: big pump fleets (Xylem/Sykes) have their own telemetry, so the gap is smaller contractors and mixed fleets. It differs from construction dewatering because the consequence is sewage flooding and regulator penalties.

title: Anti-flood non-return valves fitted to homes at risk of sewer flooding jam open between annual services
problem: Water companies fit non-return valves and pumped devices to properties on their sewer-flooding registers. Debris jams the flap and nobody knows until the next storm floods the home internally again. That brings Ofwat internal sewer-flooding penalties, compensation, clean-up costing ~£ thousands to tens of thousands per incident, and repeat victims in the local press.
who_suffers: Householders flooded with sewage; water-company customer and asset teams
buyer: Sewer flooding or customer resilience manager at a water company, with installation and maintenance through its drainage contractor
industry: Property-level sewer flood protection for homes on water-company flooding registers
current_workaround: Annual maintenance visit by a drainage contractor; otherwise the customer reports problems
sensor_concept: Reed switch on the valve flap shows its position, a float switch in the valve chamber detects surcharge, and a temperature probe is included. NB-IoT, battery. Alerts if the flap stays open in dry weather or surcharge builds, and the storm-event log proves the device worked.
notes: c1/c4 strong: Ofwat's internal sewer-flooding performance commitment carries penalties. c6 strong: drainage contractors already maintain these devices. c8 simple. c5 is an enterprise buyer, but with a budgeted programme. c7 likely unserved.

title: Blocked vortex flow controls in housing-estate SuDS tanks flood homes and roads, and management companies inspect only once or twice a year
problem: New estates drain into attenuation tanks or ponds controlled by a vortex flow control or orifice, which blocks with silt and litter. Nobody notices until a storm floods gardens, garages and roads. Management companies and adopting bodies face claims and remedial works (~£ tens of thousands), and residents dispute service charges for maintenance that wasn't done.
who_suffers: Residents; the estate management company; the drainage maintenance contractor
buyer: Operations director of a residential estate management company or of a SuDS and drainage maintenance contractor
industry: Privately managed sustainable drainage (SuDS) on new-build housing estates
current_workaround: Visual inspections and jetting every 6 or 12 months, and call-outs after flooding
sensor_concept: Ultrasonic or pressure level sensor in the flow-control chamber, plus rainfall from a public API. LTE-M/NB-IoT. Alerts when the level stays high after the rain stops (a blockage), and keeps a maintenance and storm log for residents and the adopting authority.
notes: Same pattern as the culvert-screen idea that scored 70, but a different buyer (an estate management company that bills service charges) and a different site type. c6 via drainage contractors. c8 easy. c7 likely unserved below water-company scale.

title: Continuous-flow grain dryers left running overnight at harvest: a stalled discharge or burner fault turns into a dryer and store fire
problem: At harvest, farm and co-op grain dryers run around the clock and operators get up in the night to check them. A blocked column or stalled metering roll overheats the grain, and the resulting fires destroy dryers and stores. Reported single dryer fires range from ~$26k to $850k. NFU Mutual puts UK farm fire costs at ~£100m+ a year, much of it in buildings and stored crops.
who_suffers: Arable farmers and grain-store staff losing sleep at harvest; the insurer
buyer: Farm owner or grain-store manager of an arable business or grain co-operative
industry: On-farm and central-store grain drying
sector: Grain stores, feed mills & bulk storage silos
current_workaround: An operator sits up, or sets alarms to check every 2–3 hours; older dryers rely on local thermostat cut-outs
sensor_concept: Temperature probes in the exhaust air and hot-air plenum, an accelerometer on the discharge metering roll or conveyor to confirm grain is moving, and a current clamp on the fans. LTE-M. Calls the operator's phone if temperature rises or grain stops flowing, and keeps a night-running log for the insurer.
notes: c1 strong: fire losses are large. c8 strong: cheap temperature and vibration sensing. c6 via dryer dealers' pre-harvest service visits. c7 risk: new dryers have built-in controls and GSM alarms, so the target is the large installed base of older dryers.

title: Bulk feed blown into the wrong bin on mixed livestock farms: medicated or ionophore feed reaches horses or the wrong stock
problem: Blower-lorry drivers deliver to farms with several identical bins, and a load ends up in the wrong one. It may be feed for the wrong species, medicated feed, or feed containing ionophores such as monensin, which is fatal to horses at low doses. Documented US monensin feed incidents killed ~70 horses in one case and 23+ cattle in another, with large settlements. In the UK the feed company faces claims (~£ tens of thousands) and UFAS or VMD audit findings.
who_suffers: Livestock and horse owners; the feed company's drivers and quality team
buyer: Logistics or quality (UFAS) manager at a compound feed manufacturer
industry: Bulk compound feed delivery to livestock farms
sector: Grain stores, feed mills & bulk storage silos
current_workaround: Bin numbers painted on the bins, the driver checking the delivery note, a phone call to the farmer, and padlocked lids on some farms
sensor_concept: NFC or BLE tag on each bin's fill pipe, read by a reader on the blower hose coupling (or the driver's phone), which checks the bin ID against the ticket before the blower starts. A current or pressure switch on the blower logs delivery time per bin. LTE-M. Produces proof of delivery for each bin.
notes: c1 (animal deaths, claims) and c4 (UFAS, Medicated Feed Regulations) plausible. c5/c6 strong: the feed company owns the liability and already visits. c8 simple. How often wrong-bin errors happen is unverified and needs evidence (c2/c10 risk).

title: Feed lorries arrive at pig and poultry units to find bins too full or already empty: part-loads, return trips and hungry stock
problem: UK compound feed companies schedule bulk deliveries on farmers' phoned-in estimates. If a bin is too full, the lorry leaves with a part-load and makes a return trip (~£100–£200 each). If it runs empty, birds or pigs go off feed for hours, which hurts growth and can cost birds. In North America feed mills give farms bin sensors (BinSentry and others), but UK coverage looks thin.
who_suffers: Feed-mill transport planners and drivers; pig and poultry farmers
buyer: Logistics or transport manager at a compound feed manufacturer, or feed-mill manager at an integrator
industry: Bulk feed logistics to intensive pig and poultry units
sector: Grain stores, feed mills & bulk storage silos
current_workaround: Farmers bang on the bin or climb the ladder to look, then phone in orders; drivers carry part-loads
sensor_concept: Downward ToF or ultrasonic sensor in the bin roof hatch, LTE-M. Daily level and usage forecast is pushed to the feed mill's order system, with an empty-bin alarm to the farmer.
notes: c6/c9 strong: supplier-funded telemetry, like the LPG and oil model. c7 middling: BinSentry proves willingness to pay in North America, but its UK presence needs checking. c8: ToF in dusty bins needs care. c2: deliveries are weekly.

title: Silage effluent tanks overflow after heavy rain and fresh clamping, and the effluent kills fish downstream
problem: Silage effluent is ~200 times more polluting than raw sewage (by BOD). Effluent tanks fill fast in the first weeks after clamping and after heavy rain. Overflows reach ditches and kill fish, leading to EA prosecutions (fines plus costs of several £ thousands to tens of thousands), cuts to farm payments under cross-compliance, and clean-up costs.
who_suffers: Dairy and beef farmers; the rivers and fisheries downstream
buyer: Owner or manager of a dairy or beef farm
industry: Silage clamps and effluent stores under the SSAFO Regulations
sector: Grain stores, feed mills & bulk storage silos
current_workaround: The farmer looks in the tank daily when he remembers and empties it by vacuum tanker; nobody checks at night
sensor_concept: Ultrasonic level sensor or float switch in the effluent tank, LTE-M. Alerts at high level, and logs levels and emptying to show SSAFO compliance to EA inspectors.
notes: c4/c10 strong: SSAFO, EA prosecutions, Farming Rules for Water. c8 trivial. c5 is the owner-operator. c6 weaker: could go through NFU Mutual or agricultural engineers. c7 likely unserved for effluent tanks.

title: Cement and PFA silos at concrete batching plants overfill during tanker deliveries, causing dust clouds and permit breaches
problem: Batching plants and precast yards hold LAPPC permits under process guidance PG3/1, which requires high-level alarms, pressure-relief valves and filter checks, with records. A driver blows a tanker load into a nearly full silo, the filter or relief valve blows, and a cement cloud settles on neighbours' cars. The council investigates. Costs include clean-up and claims for cars (~£ thousands), plus enforcement action or a suspended permit.
who_suffers: Plant managers; neighbours; delivery drivers
buyer: Plant manager or SHEQ manager of an independent ready-mix or precast concrete producer
industry: Bulk cement silos at concrete batching and precast plants
sector: Grain stores, feed mills & bulk storage silos
current_workaround: A local high-level probe and beacon, driver vigilance, and paper logs of filter checks
sensor_concept: Pressure transducer in the silo roof, the status of the high-level switch, and a vibration sensor on the fill line to show a delivery is in progress. LTE-M. Logs every delivery with peak pressure and level, alerts as pressure approaches the relief threshold or filter differential rises, and produces a monthly permit-compliance record.
notes: c4 strong: LAPPC permits, PG3/1, council inspection. c2: deliveries several times a week. c7: high-end silo protection systems exist for big plants, so the gap is the evidence log and small independents. c8 simple.

title: Pre-harvest welding repairs in grain stores and dryers: insurers require a fire watch after hot work that nobody carries out
problem: Every summer, farms weld conveyors, elevators and dryers before harvest. Grain dust and chaff can smoulder for hours afterwards. Insurers' hot-work conditions require a permit, a fire watch and later re-checks. A store fire is a six-figure loss, and the insurer can challenge or reduce the claim if the hot-work conditions were breached.
who_suffers: Farm and grain-store owners; agricultural engineers doing the welding
buyer: Farm owner or grain-store manager, or the agricultural engineering contractor doing the repairs
industry: Hot work in grain stores, dryers and feed mills
sector: Grain stores, feed mills & bulk storage silos
current_workaround: Paper hot-work permits where they exist at all; the welder stays a few minutes and someone has 'a look later'
sensor_concept: Portable magnetic-base sensor that combines temperature-rise and optical smoke detection, left at the work area for 4–24 hours after hot work. LTE-M. Alerts the owner and contractor, and auto-generates a fire-watch record attached to the permit.
notes: c4 (insurer hot-work conditions, standard RISCAuthority/FPA permits) and c1 (store fires) strong. c6 via agricultural engineers who do the welding. c8 simple. c7: generic hot-work monitors exist in construction, but the agricultural niche looks unserved.

title: Sugar beet clamps left uncovered on frost nights: frozen-then-thawed beet rots before haulage and the factory deducts
problem: Beet waits for weeks in field clamps for the factory's haulage slot. Growers are advised to cover clamps with fleece sheets when hard frost is forecast and to watch for heating in mild spells. Beet that freezes and then thaws rots, losing sugar and weight and causing processing problems. Deductions and rejected loads can cost ~£ thousands per clamp.
who_suffers: Beet growers; the processor's factory
buyer: Arable farm manager or beet grower, with the processor's agricultural team as a possible channel
industry: Sugar beet field clamps awaiting factory delivery
sector: Grain stores, feed mills & bulk storage silos
current_workaround: Weather forecasts, walking the clamp, and hand thermometers pushed into the heap
sensor_concept: Two or three spear temperature probes into the clamp core and surface, plus air temperature. LoRaWAN or LTE-M. Alerts when to cover against frost or when the heap is heating, and keeps a clamp log linked to delivery dates.
notes: c6 potentially strong: the single processor's agricultural staff already advise growers on storage. c8 simple. c2: daily risk over winter. c1/c4 need sourced deduction rules, so moderate. It differs from grain hot-spot monitoring in crop, buyer and the frost risk.

title: Bulk liquid fertiliser tanks on farms leak or run low unseen, and suppliers deliver on guesswork in the spraying window
problem: Liquid nitrogen fertiliser sits on farms in 20–100 t tanks, often without a bund. Slow leaks or split valves can reach watercourses, bringing EA pollution action and the loss of nitrogen worth ~£ thousands per tank. Meanwhile suppliers schedule deliveries from phone calls during the short spraying window and run emergency loads when tanks run dry.
who_suffers: Arable farmers; the supplier's logistics team; watercourses
buyer: Logistics or operations manager at a liquid fertiliser supplier, or the farm owner
industry: Bulk liquid fertiliser storage on arable farms
sector: Grain stores, feed mills & bulk storage silos
current_workaround: Sight tubes and dipping, farmer phone orders, and an annual tank inspection by the supplier
sensor_concept: Ultrasonic level sensor in the tank top, plus temperature. LTE-M. Compares usage with spraying activity and flags losses when the level falls with no spraying. The supplier gets a telemetry dashboard for refill routing.
notes: c6/c9 via supplier-owned telemetry, as in LPG and oil. c8 easy. c7 risk: generic tank gauges exist and suppliers may already use telemetry. c4 moderate: EA pollution guidance and Farming Rules for Water.

title: Mobile crushers run without dust-suppression sprays, breaching PG3/16 permits, and councils act on neighbours' dust complaints
problem: Mobile crushing and screening plant (in demolition, recycling and quarries) is permitted under LAPPC guidance PG3/16. Typical permit conditions require water sprays at the feed and discharge points whenever the plant is crushing, and crushing must stop if the water supply fails. In practice operators crush with the hose off or the bowser empty. Councils investigate dust complaints, and offences carry fines of up to £50k in the magistrates' court. There is no record that the sprays ran.
who_suffers: Neighbours and site workers; the permit holder
buyer: Managing director or compliance manager of a mobile crushing, demolition or aggregate-recycling contractor (the permit holder)
industry: Mobile crushing and screening under LAPPC permits (PG3/16)
current_workaround: The operator's word that sprays were on, paper daily checklists, and a council officer visit after complaints
sensor_concept: Pressure switch or pulse flow sensor on the spray manifold, plus an accelerometer on the crusher chassis to tell crushing from idling. LTE-M, powered from the machine's 24 V. Logs minutes crushed without water, alerts the foreman, and exports a permit-compliance record for each site move.
notes: c4 strong: statutory permit conditions, council inspections, fines. c2: daily. c8 simple. c6 via crusher dealers and hire fleets (Finlay, Sandvik, Keestrack dealers) that already fit telematics. c7 looks unserved: OEM telematics track engine hours, not sprays.

title: Quarry silt lagoons overtop in storms and send sediment into rivers, while managers check freeboard by eye
problem: Sand-and-gravel and hard-rock quarries settle wash-plant water in lagoons. Heavy rain or a stuck pump causes overtopping or a breach, discolouring rivers for kilometres. EA and SEPA prosecutions follow: quarry fines of ~£3k–£12.5k plus costs, and a housebuilder was fined £100k for a lagoon overflow. Lagoons also count as 'tips' under the Quarries Regulations 1999, which require inspections and geotechnical appraisal.
who_suffers: Quarry managers; rivers and anglers downstream
buyer: Quarry manager or estates and environment manager at an independent quarry operator
industry: Quarry settlement lagoons and site water management
current_workaround: Visual freeboard checks during shift inspections, staff driving round the lagoons in storms, and gauge boards
sensor_concept: Ultrasonic level sensor on a post above each lagoon, a float switch at the overflow or spillway, and rainfall from an API. LoRaWAN or LTE-M with solar power. Alerts when freeboard falls below the limit, and keeps a continuous level record for the tips inspection file.
notes: c1/c4/c10 decent: prosecutions with £ figures and Quarries Regulations Part 5. c2: storms monthly. c8 simple. c6 via the geotechnical and environmental consultants who inspect lagoons. c7 likely unserved below the SCADA systems of major operators.

title: Tension cracks at quarry face and tip crests: daily shift inspections miss slow movement before a collapse
problem: The Quarries Regulations 1999 require geotechnical assessment of faces and tips, plus inspections before each shift and after heavy rain. Slow movement at a face crest or tip edge gives warning signs that the eye misses. A collapse can bury plant worth ~£ hundreds of thousands or kill someone, and HSE prosecutes. Wireless geotechnical monitoring exists but is priced for large mines and rail.
who_suffers: Quarry operatives working below faces and on tips; the quarry manager
buyer: Quarry manager of an independent quarry, advised by its geotechnical specialist
industry: Face and tip stability at UK quarries
current_workaround: Visual inspections, survey prisms read periodically by surveyors, and crack pins measured with a tape
sensor_concept: MEMS tilt node or draw-wire crack meter across the tension crack. LoRaWAN or LTE-M, 5-year battery. Alerts on rate-of-movement thresholds and writes a daily record to the excavations and tips register.
notes: c4 strong: a Quarries Regulations duty with a set inspection frequency. c2: daily inspections. c8 simple. c7: a gap below enterprise systems (Senceive, Worldsensing) that needs price evidence. c1 depends on sourced incident costs.

title: Quarry wheel wash broken or bypassed: mud on the public road brings council enforcement and crash claims
problem: Planning conditions require quarries to run wheel washes and keep public roads clean. When the pump fails, the sump fills with silt or drivers bypass the wash, mud and stone spread along the highway. Councils act on planning conditions or under the Highways Act, road sweepers are hired at ~£ hundreds a day, and claims follow from motorcyclists who crash.
who_suffers: Road users; the quarry operator facing complaints and claims
buyer: Quarry manager or operations manager of an aggregates or landfill-and-quarry operator
industry: Quarry and landfill site exits
current_workaround: Weighbridge staff watch the lorries, daily visual checks, and a sweeper on call
sensor_concept: Current clamp on the wash pump, an ultrasonic sensor for tank and silt level, and a magnetometer or radar vehicle counter at the wash bay and the bypass lane. LoRaWAN or LTE-M. A daily report shows vehicles washed against vehicles that bypassed, with alerts for pump faults and a full sump.
notes: c4 (planning conditions, Highways Act s148/s149) and c10 (local press complaints) likely. c6 via wheel-wash suppliers who service the units. c8 simple. c1 needs sourced claim and fine amounts.

title: Seized conveyor pulley and idler bearings start belt fires at sand-and-gravel plants between daily belt walks
problem: A seized idler or tail-pulley bearing heats the belt until it burns or tears. A belt fire or rip stops production for days, with belt replacement costing ~£ thousands to tens of thousands plus lost output. Quarries walk their conveyors daily to meet PUWER and Quarries Regulations inspection duties, but still miss bearings that are heating up.
who_suffers: Plant fitters and operators; the quarry's production
buyer: Plant or engineering manager of an independent quarry or aggregates recycler
industry: Fixed conveyors at quarries and wash plants
current_workaround: Daily belt walks, listening, a handheld IR thermometer, and running bearings to failure
sensor_concept: Stick-on node with an accelerometer and temperature sensor on the head pulley, tail pulley and drive bearings. LoRaWAN, multi-year battery. Alerts on temperature or vibration trends, and keeps an inspection log that replaces part of the walk.
notes: c1/c2 decent. c8 simple. c7 risk: industrial wireless condition monitoring exists (SKF, Schaeffler OPTIME), so the gap is price per point for small quarries. c6 via conveyor and belting service firms.

title: Fire suppression on quarry loaders and dumpers is discharged or depressurised, and nobody knows until the machine burns
problem: Insurers commonly expect fire suppression on high-value mobile plant such as loaders and haulers worth ~£250k+. Cylinders lose pressure, actuation lines get damaged, or systems are left disarmed after maintenance. An engine-bay fire writes off the machine and stops the quarry, and insurers can challenge the claim if the system wasn't maintained.
who_suffers: Machine operators; the plant manager; the insurer
buyer: Plant manager or insurance and risk manager of a quarry operator or plant hire firm
industry: Fire suppression on mobile plant in quarries and waste sites
current_workaround: Daily operator pre-use glance at the gauge, and a 6-monthly service by the suppression installer
sensor_concept: Pressure switch or transducer on the agent or actuation cylinder, plus engine-bay temperature. Standalone LTE-M unit on the machine's 24 V, with no CAN integration. Alerts on pressure loss or discharge, and sends the insurer a monthly 'armed' report.
notes: c4 via insurer requirements. c6 strong: suppression installers service every 6 months. c8 simple. c7 risk: some suppression brands offer on-board monitoring panels, though remote logging is less common.

title: Haul-road water bowsers sit idle on dry, windy days, breaching quarry dust-management planning conditions
problem: Mineral planning permissions require dust management schemes, which include damping haul roads in dry weather. The bowser sits idle when its driver is moved to another job. Dust reaches nearby houses, complaints pile up at liaison meetings, and councils or the EA take action or object to extensions. There is no record of when the roads were damped.
who_suffers: Neighbours; the quarry manager defending the operation
buyer: Quarry manager or environment manager of a quarry or landfill operator
industry: Haul-road dust suppression at quarries
current_workaround: Driver logbook, the manager's visual checks, and a complaints log
sensor_concept: GPS tracker and pulse flow sensor on the bowser spray bar, plus wind and humidity from a cheap on-site weather sensor. LTE-M. Maps which roads were damped against the weather, alerts when it is dry and windy and the bowser hasn't sprayed, and produces a monthly compliance report for liaison meetings.
notes: c4 (planning conditions, dust management plans) and c10 (community liaison complaints) plausible. c8 simple. c7 likely unserved: generic GPS tracks the vehicle, not spraying against weather. c1 weak unless a refused extension or a fine is sourced.

title: Wash-plant flocculant dosing stops when the hopper or drum runs out, and dirty water reaches the lagoons and discharge point
problem: Wash plants and silt presses dose flocculant to settle fines. When the powder hopper or liquid drum runs out, or the dosing pump trips, the fines don't settle. The water circuit turns dirty, product goes out of spec, and silty water can reach the consented discharge. Lost production and re-washing cost ~£ thousands per shift, on top of the permit risk.
who_suffers: Wash-plant operators; the quarry's sales and environmental compliance
buyer: Plant manager at an aggregates or construction-and-demolition recycling wash plant
industry: Aggregate washing plants and water recycling
current_workaround: The operator checks the hopper level each shift; dosing-pump alarms sound only in the control cabin
sensor_concept: Load cell or tilt-level sensor on the flocculant hopper or drum, plus a current clamp on the dosing pump. LoRaWAN or LTE-M. Alerts on low stock and on the pump stopping, and logs consumption for the flocculant supplier, which can then auto-replenish.
notes: c6/c9 via the service model of flocculant chemical suppliers. c8 simple. c7 likely unserved. Resembles the biocide-drum idea (R01-B-02) but sits in quarries with a different buyer.

title: Trespassers swim in flooded quarries every summer, and operators pay for security patrols and face drowning inquests
problem: In every hot spell, young people swim in cold, deep quarry lakes. Drownings are reported most summers and coroners criticise access control. Operators pay for security patrols (~£ hundreds per night) and fencing repairs, and carry Occupiers' Liability and reputational exposure.
who_suffers: Young swimmers and their families; quarry operators and restoration landowners
buyer: Estates or security manager of a quarry operator with working or restored lakes
industry: Flooded working and restored quarries
current_workaround: Fencing, signs, paid weekend patrols, and calls to the police
sensor_concept: PIR or microwave presence sensor at known access points with a pre-recorded loudspeaker warning. LTE-M alert to the patrol with a time log. Solar powered.
notes: c10 strong: drownings in the press every year and RoSPA campaigns. c3: paid patrols. c8 simple. c1/c5 weaker because deaths are not a priced loss to the operator; included as a long shot.

title: Inflatable hirers leave bouncy castles with customers as the wind rises, and nobody measures the wind or notices the blower stop
problem: HSE guidance says no inflatable should be used in winds above 24 mph and that wind should be checked with an anemometer at regular intervals. At parties, fêtes and fairs, the operator often leaves the hirer in charge. A gust lifts the unit, or a tripped blower collapses it on children. In the Harlow case (2016), two operators were jailed for 3 years for gross negligence manslaughter after failing to monitor the wind. Insurance and PIPA inspection exist, but there is no proof that wind checks happened.
who_suffers: Children on the equipment; hire-company owners carrying criminal and civil liability
buyer: Owner of an inflatable hire business (PIPA or BIHA member)
industry: Inflatable play equipment hire for parties, fêtes and events
current_workaround: A handheld anemometer if the operator is present, weather apps, and telling the hirer to 'deflate if windy'
sensor_concept: Low-cost cup anemometer on a short mast clipped to the unit, a current sensor or air-pressure switch on the blower, and an accelerometer on an anchor point. LTE-M. Sends SMS and voice-call alerts to the hirer and operator above 20 or 24 mph or when the blower stops, and keeps a hire log for the insurer and PIPA.
notes: c4/c10 strong: HSE guidance, a manslaughter conviction, press coverage. c2: every hire. c5: owner-operator. c6 via PIPA, insurers and manufacturers. c8 simple. c7: cheap handheld anemometers exist, but nothing gives a remote alert or a log.

title: Long-hire marquees at pubs, restaurants and Christmas venues stand unattended through storms, and the hire company hears about damage from the client
problem: Since COVID, many venues hire marquees and stretch tents for months at a time. IStructE guidance on temporary demountable structures calls for a wind management plan with thresholds for inspection and evacuation, but out of hours nobody is watching. Storms rip covers, pull pegs and wreck frames (~£ thousands to £ tens of thousands per marquee), and a collapse onto guests brings HSE or council action.
who_suffers: Venue guests and staff; marquee hire companies
buyer: Operations director of a marquee or stretch-tent hire company (MUTA member)
industry: Long-term marquee and temporary structure hire
current_workaround: Met Office warnings, phone calls from clients, and inspection visits after storms
sensor_concept: Mast-mounted anemometer plus accelerometer or tilt nodes on two frame legs or king poles to detect movement and uplift. LTE-M. Alerts the venue and hire company at the gust thresholds in the wind plan and on frame movement, and sends a post-storm report of which sites need a visit.
notes: c4 (IStructE temporary structures guidance, wind management plans, licensing safety conditions) and c6 (the hire company visits and maintains) strong. c2: storms monthly in winter. c8 simple. c7 likely unserved for small hire firms.

title: Festival sewage holding tanks leak or overflow into streams; Glastonbury paid £31k after 42 fish died
problem: Greenfield festivals hold toilet waste and urine in temporary steel or plastic tanks. A leak or overfill reaches watercourses. Glastonbury Festival was ordered to pay ~£31k in 2016 after a tank leaked ~20,000 gallons into the Whitelake River and killed 42 fish. Event pollution plans require containment, yet tank levels are checked by eye, and in that case the EA's river sensors spotted the leak first.
who_suffers: Festival organisers; rivers and fisheries; licence holders facing prosecution
buyer: Site or production manager or licence holder of a greenfield festival, or the toilet and waste contractor
industry: Greenfield music festivals and large temporary events
current_workaround: Tanker crews dip tanks on their rounds, visual walk-rounds, and EA watercourse monitoring
sensor_concept: Ultrasonic level sensor on each holding tank, plus water-presence or float sensors in bunds and nearby drains. LTE-M, or a LoRaWAN gateway on site. Alerts on overfill, unexplained level drops (leaks) and liquid in bunds, and keeps an incident log for the EA.
notes: c1/c4/c10 strong: a named EA prosecution with a £ figure, and the Glastonbury case was widely reported. c6 via toilet and waste contractors already on site. c8 simple. c2: daily during each event. c9 weaker because events are seasonal, so a hire model fits.

title: Outdoor concerts break licensed off-site noise limits, and complaints and licence reviews arrive before the sound engineer knows
problem: Premises licences set off-site noise limits, for example LAeq over 15 minutes at the nearest homes under the concerts code of practice. Smaller festivals and outdoor venues can't afford continuous monitoring by a consultant. Breaches lead to complaints, licence reviews, earlier curfews and fines, and festivals have lost their licences.
who_suffers: Neighbours; festival promoters and outdoor venues at risk of losing licences
buyer: Production manager or licence holder of a mid-size festival or outdoor event venue
industry: Outdoor concerts, festivals and event venues with noise conditions on their licence
current_workaround: A noise consultant with Class 1 meters at big events; at smaller ones, someone walking round with a handheld meter, or nothing
sensor_concept: Weatherproof indicative noise nodes with MEMS microphones (not Class 1) at 3–6 sensitive receptors, LTE-M. Live LAeq and LCeq go to the front-of-house desk with traffic-light thresholds, and a daily evidence pack is backed by consultant spot checks.
notes: c4 strong: licence conditions. c10 strong: complaints and licence reviews in the press. c6 via noise consultants and sound rental companies. c8 moderate: non-Class-1 accuracy may limit use as evidence. c7: professional terminals are expensive and hire-only.

title: Festival tents and arenas go over their licensed capacity while stewards count with clickers
problem: Licences and event safety plans set a capacity for each tent and arena. Stewards close entrances on guesswork and hand clickers. Overcrowding causes crush injuries, breaches licence conditions and brings post-event licence reviews, which can put the whole festival at risk of closure.
who_suffers: Festival-goers; stewards; the licence holder
buyer: Head of safety or crowd-management lead at a festival, or at a crowd-management contractor
industry: Festival tents, arenas and temporary venues with capacity limits
current_workaround: Hand clickers, visual estimates of crowd density, and CCTV analysis at big events
sensor_concept: Battery-powered bidirectional counters (IR beam-break or ToF) on tent entrances and exits, with a LoRaWAN gateway. Shows live occupancy per tent on a phone dashboard with alerts at 80%, 90% and 100%, and produces a post-event report for the licensing authority.
notes: c4 (licence capacity conditions, Purple Guide) and c10 (crush incidents) strong. c6 via crowd-management companies. c8 simple. c7 risk from retail people counters and enterprise crowd analytics.

title: Water-filled ballast under stages, PA towers and marquee legs leaks away mid-event
problem: On hard ground, temporary structures are held down by water-filled ballast tanks (IBC type) sized by the structural engineer. Leaks, vandalism, or staff draining a tank for water leave less ballast than designed, and in high wind towers, banners and marquee legs lift. Collapses injure people and lead to HSE or council action and claims.
who_suffers: Audiences and crew; staging suppliers and event organisers
buyer: Technical or production manager at a staging or temporary structure supplier
industry: Temporary demountable structures on hard standing at events
current_workaround: Daily visual check of the ballast tanks during the build and on show days
sensor_concept: Float or ultrasonic level sensor (or a simple pressure switch) in each ballast tank, plus a tamper accelerometer. LoRaWAN. Alarms if any tank drops below its design weight, and keeps a ballast-check log for the structural engineer's sign-off.
notes: c4 (IStructE temporary structures guidance requires ballast checks) and c8 (trivial sensor) strong. c6 via staging suppliers. c7 likely unserved. c1/c10 depend on finding specific incident cases.

title: Seasonal temporary ice rinks: a chiller or glycol pump trips overnight and the ice is slush by opening time
problem: Seasonal rinks at castles, shopping centres and city squares run on hired chillers and glycol mats. A tripped chiller, a stopped generator or a pump fault overnight softens the ice. Sessions are cancelled (~£ thousands per day in ticket refunds) and re-freezing takes a day. Operators employ night staff to watch the plant.
who_suffers: Rink operators; ticket holders; host venues
buyer: Operations director of a seasonal ice rink operator
industry: Temporary seasonal ice rinks
current_workaround: A night technician, the chiller's local alarm, and morning checks
sensor_concept: Clamp-on temperature sensors on the glycol flow and return, an IR sensor for ice-surface temperature, and a current clamp on the chiller supply. LTE-M. Alerts the on-call engineer when glycol temperature rises, and keeps a season log.
notes: c1/c2 moderate: lost sessions. c3: night staff. c8 simple. c7 risk: chiller hire firms offer their own telemetry, so the gap is mixed fleets and the operator's own view.

title: Pull-cord alarms in accessible toilets at events only buzz locally, so a disabled visitor who falls goes unheard
problem: Hired accessible toilet units have emergency pull-cord alarms, but at festivals and outdoor events they only sound a local buzzer in a noisy field. Cords get tied up and batteries go flat. A disabled visitor who falls waits unheard. Equality Act complaints, bad reviews and licensing complaints follow.
who_suffers: Disabled visitors; festival accessibility teams; toilet hire companies
buyer: Ops director of a portable toilet hire company, or a festival's accessibility lead
industry: Accessible temporary toilet units at events
current_workaround: A local buzzer, stewards passing by, and checks during cleaning rounds
sensor_concept: Pull-cord switch and reset button wired to a LoRa or LTE-M module. Alerts stewards' radios or phones with the unit's location, runs a daily self-test, and detects a tied-up cord (continuously open).
notes: c8 trivial. c6 via toilet hire firms. c7 likely unserved. Weak on c1 (no £5k figure) and c4 (guidance-based, not statutory at events), so a long shot.

title: Nursery garden gates and side doors left open: toddlers walk out unnoticed and Ofsted suspends the setting
problem: The EYFS statutory framework requires premises to be secure so children can't leave unsupervised. UK cases keep recurring: toddlers found alone in parks or on roads after leaving through an unlocked gate or side door. Ofsted suspended nurseries in Walthamstow, Thurrock and Carshalton while it investigated. Suspension means weeks of lost fee income (~£ tens of thousands for a 60-place setting), plus downgrades and lost enrolments.
who_suffers: Young children and parents; nursery staff facing disciplinary action; the nursery owner
buyer: Owner or operations director of a multi-site nursery group
industry: Private day nurseries and early-years settings in England (EYFS/Ofsted)
current_workaround: Staff told to check gates, a magnetic lock on the main door only, walk-round checks and risk assessments
sensor_concept: Reed or magnetic contacts on outdoor play gates, fire exits and side doors, with a LoRaWAN or LTE-M hub. A chime and phone or tablet alert goes to room leaders if a gate stays open for more than 10 s during session hours. Keeps a daily open/close log for Ofsted and the insurer.
notes: c4 strong: EYFS statutory framework and Ofsted suspensions. c10 strong: many press cases. c5: owner-operator groups with budget. c8 trivial. c6 via nursery insurers or nursery management software (Famly, Blossom). c7 seems unserved: door-entry systems cover only the front door.

title: Schools keeping RAAC roof planks must monitor deflection, but engineers measure by hand a few times a year
problem: Since 2023, schools and colleges that keep RAAC in place must manage and monitor it. Deflection of span/100 or more (~40 mm on a 4 m plank) is the most serious warning category in published guidance. Monitoring relies on engineers' periodic visits, and between visits a plank can deflect after a roof leak. The 2023 closures forced schools into temporary classrooms and emergency propping at ~£ tens of thousands each.
who_suffers: Pupils and staff under RAAC roofs; trust estates teams
buyer: Estates director of a multi-academy trust, or a local-authority or diocesan property lead, reached via the structural engineering consultancy
industry: School and college buildings with RAAC under monitoring
current_workaround: Periodic engineer inspections with laser measures, propping, and staff reporting cracks and leaks
sensor_concept: Ceiling-mounted ToF laser distance sensor (VL53 class) or MEMS tilt node on each critical plank, plus a moisture spot sensor in the roof void. LoRaWAN or NB-IoT, multi-year battery. Alerts on deflection rate or threshold, and sends the engineer a monthly report.
notes: c4/c10 strong: DfE and IStructE RAAC guidance, national news. c6 via structural engineers doing RAAC surveys. c8 simple. c7: some structural-monitoring firms offer RAAC monitoring at enterprise prices, which needs checking. c2: monitoring is monthly.

title: Water leaks in empty schools run for days over the holidays: flooded classrooms and RPA escape-of-water claims
problem: Schools are empty for ~13 weeks a year. A burst pipe, failed float valve or overflowing roof tank runs unseen until staff return. Ceilings collapse, IT is ruined and rooms close. Escape of water is one of the costlier claim types for the academies' Risk Protection Arrangement and for local-authority school insurers (~£ tens of thousands per incident).
who_suffers: Pupils and staff losing rooms; trust estates teams; the RPA or insurer
buyer: Estates or facilities manager of a multi-academy trust
industry: School estates during holidays and weekends
current_workaround: Site-manager walk-rounds in the holidays, monthly meter readings, and water bills noticed weeks later
sensor_concept: Optical pulse reader on the main water meter alarms when water flows outside the school timetable, plus 2–4 spot leak sensors in plant rooms and roof tanks. LTE-M. Calendar-aware alarms go to the trust's estates team.
notes: c1 (escape-of-water claim costs) and c5 (MAT estates budgets) good. c8 simple. c6 via water retailers or the RPA/insurer. c7 risk: generic leak detection is crowded, so the niche is the calendar-aware trust dashboard.

title: Wheelie bins pushed against school buildings out of hours start arson fires that destroy classrooms
problem: Insurers' school fire guidance says bins should be locked away ~6–8 m from buildings, because arson often starts in bins pushed against walls. A school fire costs ~£ hundreds of thousands to millions and closes classrooms for months. RPA and local-authority insurers push schools on bin management.
who_suffers: Pupils displaced by fire; trust estates teams; insurers
buyer: Estates or site manager of a multi-academy trust or independent school, encouraged by the RPA or insurer
industry: Arson prevention on school estates
current_workaround: Bin compounds, chains and padlocks, and the site manager's evening checks
sensor_concept: Tilt, motion and temperature sensor inside each bin lid, plus BLE proximity to a gateway in the bin compound to detect a bin leaving it. LoRaWAN or LTE-M. Alerts out of hours when a bin is moved or heats up, and keeps a weekly 'bins secured' log for the insurer.
notes: c1 strong: school fire losses are large and documented by insurers. c4: insurer guidance and the RPA. c8 simple, but location precision needs care. c2 weak (rare per school), so pitch it as a weekly evidence log.

title: Multi-academy trusts can't prove each school's weekly fire-alarm test happened, and auditors and fire officers find the gaps
problem: BS 5839-1 and fire risk assessments expect a weekly call-point test recorded in the fire logbook. Across 10–40 schools, site staff skip weeks and logbooks go missing. The trust's central estates team only finds out at audit or after a fire-service visit, and enforcement notices and insurer challenges follow. A fire with a non-working alarm would leave the trust exposed.
who_suffers: Trust estates and compliance teams; site staff; pupils if an alarm fails
buyer: Head of estates or compliance manager of a multi-academy trust
industry: Fire safety compliance across multi-academy trusts
current_workaround: Paper fire logbooks, compliance software where staff tick boxes, and termly audits
sensor_concept: Plug-in acoustic sensor near a sounder that recognises the alarm tone pattern, or a volt-free relay input from the panel's sounder circuit. LTE-M. Auto-logs every test with its duration, flags missed weeks, and feeds a trust-wide dashboard.
notes: Pairs a statutory weekly check (the pattern that scored 69 for HMOs) with a budget-holding central buyer (MAT estates). c6 via fire-alarm maintenance contractors who visit every 6 months. c8 simple. c7 likely unserved: compliance apps rely on manual entry.

title: School boilers fail overnight and the head finds out at 7 am: cold classrooms, closures and emergency call-outs
problem: In older schools without a BMS, a boiler lockout or pump failure on a winter night leaves classrooms cold by morning. Schools send pupils home or close: each closure day costs ~£ thousands in staff time, hurts attendance and draws parent complaints. On top come emergency call-out rates.
who_suffers: Pupils and staff; heads managing closures; trust estates teams
buyer: Estates manager of a multi-academy trust, or the heating maintenance contractor that holds the schools' PPM contract
industry: School heating plant without a BMS
current_workaround: The caretaker arrives early to check, and the school calls out a contractor reactively
sensor_concept: Clamp-on pipe temperature sensors on flow and return, a current clamp on the circulation pump, and 2–3 classroom temperature tags. LTE-M. If flow temperature hasn't risen on schedule, the contractor gets an alert at 4 am. Also sends a monthly plant-health report.
notes: c5/c6 good: the contractor already visits and can sell it. c8 simple. c2: weekly risk in winter. c7 risk from BMS and energy-monitoring firms. c1 needs a sourced closure cost.

title: Exam-paper secure rooms opened outside authorised windows, and centres can't show JCQ inspectors an access record
problem: JCQ rules require exam papers to be kept in a secure room or safe with restricted keyholders, and centres are inspected on this. Paper leaks or early openings lead to malpractice investigations, sanctions on the centre, and the cost of replacement papers for awarding bodies. Centres rely on handwritten logs.
who_suffers: Exams officers; heads; candidates if papers are compromised
buyer: School business manager or exams officer, or a MAT exams lead
industry: Examination centres in schools and colleges
current_workaround: Handwritten access log, keys held by the exams officer, and CCTV in some centres
sensor_concept: Reed contacts on the secure-room door and the safe, LTE-M. Alerts on openings outside timetabled windows, and exports a tamper-evident access log for the JCQ inspection.
notes: c4 strong: JCQ rules and the annual inspection. c8 trivial. c7 likely unserved. Weak on c1 and c5 (small budgets), so a long shot.

title: Radon sump fans in schools in radon Affected Areas fail silently, letting levels climb back above the action level
problem: Under the Ionising Radiations Regulations 2017, employers in radon Affected Areas must measure radon and act above 300 Bq/m³. Many schools fixed it with a radon sump and fan. If the fan fails or someone switches it off, levels rise again unnoticed until the next 3-month test, if one happens at all. HSE expects remediation to be kept working.
who_suffers: Staff and pupils exposed to radon; school H&S leads
buyer: Estates or H&S manager of a MAT or local-authority school estate in radon areas (e.g. Cornwall, Devon, Derbyshire, Northamptonshire)
industry: Radon remediation systems in schools
current_workaround: Occasional checks of a U-tube manometer on the pipe, and periodic retests with passive detectors
sensor_concept: Differential pressure switch or current clamp on the sump fan, with an optional low-cost radon sensor. LoRaWAN or LTE-M. Alerts on fan failure and issues a monthly 'system operating' certificate.
notes: c4 solid: IRR17 and UKHSA guidance. c8 very simple (a pressure switch). c7 likely unserved. c6 via radon remediation contractors. c1/c2 weak: the harm is long-term health, not a priced incident.
